lemma instFiniteSound_of_instSound {C : FrameClass} {FC : FiniteFrameClass} (heq : C.restrictFinite = FC) [sound : Sound H C] : Sound H FC := ⟨by
  /-
    H : LO.Modal.Hilbert Nat
    C : LO.Modal.Kripke.FrameClass
    FC : LO.Modal.Kripke.FiniteFrameClass
    heq : Eq C.restrictFinite FC
    sound : LO.Sound H C
    ⊢ ∀ {f : LO.Modal.Formula Nat}, LO.System.Provable H f → LO.Semantics.Realize  …
  -/
  intro φ hφ F hF;
  /-
    H : LO.Modal.Hilbert Nat
    C : LO.Modal.Kripke.FrameClass
    FC : LO.Modal.Kripke.FiniteFrameClass
    heq : Eq C.restrictFinite FC
    sound : LO.Sound H C
    φ : LO.Modal.Formula Nat
    hφ : LO.System.Provable H φ
    F : LO.Modal.Kripke.Frame
    hF : Membership.mem FC.toFrameClass F
    ⊢ LO.Semantics.Realize F φ
  -/
  apply sound.sound (f := φ) hφ;
  /-
    H : LO.Modal.Hilbert Nat
    C : LO.Modal.Kripke.FrameClass
    FC : LO.Modal.Kripke.FiniteFrameClass
    heq : Eq C.restrictFinite FC
    sound : LO.Sound H C
    φ : LO.Modal.Formula Nat
    hφ : LO.System.Provable H φ
    F : LO.Modal.Kripke.Frame
    hF : Membership.mem FC.toFrameClass F
    ⊢ Membership.mem C F
  -/
  rw [←heq] at hF;
  /-
    H : LO.Modal.Hilbert Nat
    C : LO.Modal.Kripke.FrameClass
    FC : LO.Modal.Kripke.FiniteFrameClass
    heq : Eq C.restrictFinite FC
    sound : LO.Sound H C
    φ : LO.Modal.Formula Nat
    hφ : LO.System.Provable H φ
    F : LO.Modal.Kripke.Frame
    hF : Membership.mem C.restrictFinite.toFrameClass F
    ⊢ Membership.mem C F
  -/
  simp [FrameClass.restrictFinite, FiniteFrameClass.toFrameClass] at hF;
  /-
    H : LO.Modal.Hilbert Nat
    C : LO.Modal.Kripke.FrameClass
    FC : LO.Modal.Kripke.FiniteFrameClass
    heq : Eq C.restrictFinite FC
    sound : LO.Sound H C
    φ : LO.Modal.Formula Nat
    hφ : LO.System.Provable H φ
    F : LO.Modal.Kripke.Frame
    hF : Exists fun x => And (Membership.mem C x.toFrame) (Eq x.toFrame F)
    ⊢ Membership.mem C F
  -/
  obtain ⟨F, hF, rfl⟩ := hF;
  /-
    case intro.intro
    H : LO.Modal.Hilbert Nat
    C : LO.Modal.Kripke.FrameClass
    FC : LO.Modal.Kripke.FiniteFrameClass
    heq : Eq C.restrictFinite FC
    sound : LO.Sound H C
    φ : LO.Modal.Formula Nat
    hφ : LO.System.Provable H φ
    F : LO.Modal.Kripke.FiniteFrame
    hF : Membership.mem C F.toFrame
    ⊢ Membership.mem C F.toFrame
  -/

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

C1_dependencies.content:
/-- Useful induction for normal modal logic. -/
noncomputable def inducition_with_necOnly! [H.HasNecOnly]
  {motive  : (φ : Formula α) → H ⊢! φ → Prop}
  (hMaxm   : ∀ {φ}, (h : φ ∈ H.axioms) → motive φ ⟨maxm h⟩)
  (hMdp    : ∀ {φ ψ}, {hpq : H ⊢! φ ➝ ψ} → {hp : H ⊢! φ} → motive (φ ➝ ψ) hpq → motive φ hp → motive ψ (hpq ⨀ hp))
  (hNec    : ∀ {φ}, {hp : H ⊢! φ} → (ihp : motive φ hp) → motive (□φ) (System.nec! hp))
  (hImply₁   : ∀ {φ ψ}, motive (φ ➝ ψ ➝ φ) $ ⟨imply₁ φ ψ⟩)
  (hImply₂   : ∀ {φ ψ χ}, motive ((φ ➝ ψ ➝ χ) ➝ (φ ➝ ψ) ➝ φ ➝ χ) $ ⟨imply₂ φ ψ χ⟩)
  (hElimContra : ∀ {φ ψ}, motive (Axioms.ElimContra φ ψ) $ ⟨ec φ ψ⟩)
  : ∀ {φ}, (d : H ⊢! φ) → motive φ d := by
  intro φ d;
  induction d using Deduction.inducition! with
  | hMaxm h => exact hMaxm h
  | hMdp ihpq ihp => exact hMdp (ihpq) (ihp);
  | hRules rl hrl hant ih =>
    rw [HasNecOnly.has_necessitation_only] at hrl;
    obtain ⟨φ, rfl⟩ := hrl;
    exact @hNec φ (hant (by simp)) $ ih (by simp);
  | hImply₁ => exact hImply₁
  | hImply₂ => exact hImply₂
  | hElimContra => exact hElimContra

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

C1_dependencies.name: LO.Modal.Hilbert.Deduction.inducition_with_necOnly!
C1_dependencies.content:
/-- Useful induction for normal modal logic. -/
noncomputable def inducition_with_necOnly! [H.HasNecOnly]
  {motive  : (φ : Formula α) → H ⊢! φ → Prop}
  (hMaxm   : ∀ {φ}, (h : φ ∈ H.axioms) → motive φ ⟨maxm h⟩)
  (hMdp    : ∀ {φ ψ}, {hpq : H ⊢! φ ➝ ψ} → {hp : H ⊢! φ} → motive (φ ➝ ψ) hpq → motive φ hp → motive ψ (hpq ⨀ hp))
  (hNec    : ∀ {φ}, {hp : H ⊢! φ} → (ihp : motive φ hp) → motive (□φ) (System.nec! hp))
  (hImply₁   : ∀ {φ ψ}, motive (φ ➝ ψ ➝ φ) $ ⟨imply₁ φ ψ⟩)
  (hImply₂   : ∀ {φ ψ χ}, motive ((φ ➝ ψ ➝ χ) ➝ (φ ➝ ψ) ➝ φ ➝ χ) $ ⟨imply₂ φ ψ χ⟩)
  (hElimContra : ∀ {φ ψ}, motive (Axioms.ElimContra φ ψ) $ ⟨ec φ ψ⟩)
  : ∀ {φ}, (d : H ⊢! φ) → motive φ d := by
  intro φ d;
  induction d using Deduction.inducition! with
  | hMaxm h => exact hMaxm h
  | hMdp ihpq ihp => exact hMdp (ihpq) (ihp);
  | hRules rl hrl hant ih =>
    rw [HasNecOnly.has_necessitation_only] at hrl;
    obtain ⟨φ, rfl⟩ := hrl;
    exact @hNec φ (hant (by simp)) $ ih (by simp);
  | hImply₁ => exact hImply₁
  | hImply₂ => exact hImply₂
  | hElimContra => exact hElimContra

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

-/

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

informal_statement: If two modal logics are both sound and complete with respect to the same Hilbert-Extended Kripke semantics, then the logics themselves are equivalent.
informal_proof:
Let \( L_1 \) and \( L_2 \) be two modal logics with respective axiomatizations Ax₁ and Ax₂. Suppose both logics are equipped with the same Hilbert-Extended Kripke semantics, denoted by \( C_1 \) and \( C_2 \), respectively. 

Given that \( C_1 = C_2 \), and both logics are sound, it means that every theorem of \( L_1 \) is valid in \( C_1 \), and every theorem of \( L_2 \) is valid in \( C_2 \). Since \( C_1 \) and \( C_2 \) are identical, the set of valid formulas for \( L_1 \) and \( L_2 \) coincide.

Furthermore, as both logics are complete, any valid formula in \( C_1 \) (and thus in \( C_2 \)) is a theorem of \( L_1 \) and \( L_2 \). Therefore, the sets of theorems of \( L_1 \) and \( L_2 \) are equal. This implies that \( L_1 = L_2 \), meaning the two logics are equivalent.

informal_statement: If the class of Kripke frames \( C_2 \) is a subset of \( C_1 \), and the Hilbert system with axioms \( Ax_2 \) is complete with respect to \( C_2 \), while the system with \( Ax_1 \) is both sound and complete with respect to \( C_1 \), then the logic with \( Ax_1 \) is weaker than the one with \( Ax_2 \).
informal_proof:
Given that \( C_2 \subseteq C_1 \), every model in \( C_2 \) is also a model in \( C_1 \). 

Since the Hilbert system with \( Ax_2 \) is complete with respect to \( C_2 \), any formula provable in this system is true in all models in \( C_2 \). Because all models in \( C_2 \) are also in \( C_1 \), this formula is true in all models of \( C_1 \).

The Hilbert system with \( Ax_1 \) is sound and complete with respect to \( C_1 \). Therefore, since the formula is true in all models of \( C_1 \), it is provable in the system with \( Ax_1 \).

Hence, every formula provable in the system with \( Ax_2 \) is also provable in the system with \( Ax_1 \), which means the system with \( Ax_1 \) is weaker than the system with \( Ax_2 \).

Through this methodology, we conclude that \( K(\mathbb{N}) \) does not lead to any contradictions, thereby confirming its consistency.

informal_proof:
To establish the soundness of Kripke semantics for the Hilbert-style calculus K in modal logic, we proceed as follows:

1. **Semantic Validity**: Kripke semantics models the concepts of necessity and possibility through possible worlds and accessibility relations. For calculus K, the accessibility relation is typically reflexive and transitive, aligning with the axioms of K.

2. **aligned Fragments**: The Hilbert-style calculus K includes axioms such as Necessitation, K (分配律), and T (Reflexivity). These correspond appropriately to the Kripke semantics properties, ensuring that each axiom is validated in all Kripke models.

3. **Soundness of Completeness**: By design, the semantic definitions (such as validity in a model) and the axiomatic system (K) are aligned. Meaning, every theorem in K is valid in all Kripke models, which directly translates to the soundness of the system.

4. **Formal Proof Mechanism**: The Lean4 code provided indicates that a soundness proof is instantiated for the specific case of all frames, denoted by AllFrameClass. This leverages the underlying properties of frames and the defined semantics to confirm that the system is sound.

5. **Conclusion**: Therefore, since each axiom and derived rule in the Hilbert-style K calculus is validated in all Kripke models, the entire calculus is sound with respect to these semantics.

<STATEMENT>

There exists a consistent logical system or class $HC$ within the context of a nonempty finite frameclass $FC$.

</STATEMENT>

<PROOF>

To establish the consistency of the logical system or class $HC$ within the context of a nonempty finite frameclass $FC$, we employ a proof by contradiction. Assume, for the sake of contradiction, that $HC$ is inconsistent. This would mean that there exists a formula $\phi$ such that both $HC \vdash \phi$ and $HC \vdash \neg\phi$ hold. However, this leads to a direct contradiction since a consistent system cannot prove both a statement and its negation simultaneously. Therefore, our initial assumption must be false, and thus $HC$ is consistent within the given frameclass $FC$.

informal_statement: Any formula that is always realizable is not a contradiction. Equivalently, every non-contradictory formula is realizable.
informal_proof:
Assume that a formula is not a contradiction. By definition, this means it is not always false. Therefore, there exists a model where the formula is true.

Britti Fine, the system's soundness ensures that if a formula is realizable, it is not a contradiction. Therefore, if a formula is not a contradiction, it must be realizable in some model.

Zenon Fine, a specific frame or model, serves as a witness for the realizability of the formula. Since the frame is nonempty, it provides the necessary structure to interpret the formula in a meaningful way.

Using the Kripke semantics, we can interpret the formula within Zenon Fine. Because Zenon Fine is a valid model, the formula is realized in it, confirming its realizability. Hence, the assumption that the formula is not a contradiction leads us to conclude that it is indeed realizable.

informal_statement: If a formula `$\phi$` is provable in Hilbert's calculus under the conditions defined by `FC`, then `$\phi$` is valid in the semantics of `FC`.
informal_proof:
Assume that `$\phi$` is provable in Hilbert's calculus under the specified conditions defined by `FC`. 

We begin by considering an arbitrary model or interpretation that satisfies `FC`. Since `$\phi$` is provable in Hilbert's calculus, it must hold in all such interpretations. By the soundness of Hilbert's calculus, `$\phi$` is therefore true in every model governed by `FC`.

To establish validity in `FC`, we proceed by induction on the number of steps required to prove `$\phi$` in Hilbert's system. 

- **Base Case**: If `$\phi$` is an axiom or a direct inference from the axioms, it is trivially valid in `FC` by the definition of `FC`.
  
- **Inductive Step**: Assume that all formulas derived in fewer steps than `$\phi$` are valid in `FC`. Consider a formula derived from `$\phi$`. By the inductive hypothesis and the rules of inference in `FC`, the derived formula must also be valid in `FC`.

Thus, by induction, `$\phi$` is valid in `FC`, concluding that FC ⊧ φ whenever Hilbert's calculus proves φ under the given conditions.

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

informal_proof:
We begin by acknowledging the given condition of having a nonempty frameclass, which serves as a foundational structure within our system. Given the `Sound H C` property, we know that valid derivations within `H` correspond to realizable properties in the frameclass. 

To demonstrate that `H` does not entail the contradiction symbol `⊥`, we rely on the existence of this nonempty frameclass. By the definition of soundness, if `H` were to entail `⊥`, it would imply that `⊥` is realizable in every frameclass, including our nonempty one. However, `⊥` is not realizable in any nonempty frameclass, as it symbolizes an impossible condition. 

Therefore, the existence of a nonempty frameclass confirms that `H` does not entail `⊥`, preserving the consistency of the system.

informal_statement: For a given Hilbert space \( H \), if \( H \) is defined exactly as a Hilbert space of context \( C \), then the system is sound concerning context \( C \).
informal_proof:
Suppose we have a Hilbert space \( H \) and a context \( C \). We aim to show that if \( H \) is defined as the Hilbert space of \( C \), then the system is sound with respect to \( C \).

First, let \( \varphi \) be an arbitrary formula and assume that \( \varphi \) holds in \( H \), denoted as \( H \vDash \varphi \). Our goal is to show that \( C \vDash \varphi \), meaning \( \varphi \) also holds in the context \( C \).

Given that \( H \) is defined as the Hilbert space of \( C \), we can apply the auxiliary lemma `instSound_of_frameClass_definedBy_aux`, which connects the soundness of \( H \) and the context \( C \). Specifically, using the definition of equality `heq`, we infer that \( C \) correctly captures the properties of \( H \).

By applying the auxiliary lemma and leveraging the definition of `heq`, we establish that \( C \) ensures the soundness of \( \varphi \) just as \( H \) does. Therefore, \( C \vDash \varphi \) follows directly from these considerations.

Since \( \varphi \) was an arbitrary formula, this demonstrates that the system remains sound concerning the context \( C \).

informal_proof:
To prove that if φ is derivable in the Hilbert system with `ExtK`, then φ holds in the class C, we proceed as follows:

1. **Assumption**: Assume that φ is a theorem of the Hilbert system with `ExtK`, denoted as `Hilbert.ExtK ⊢! φ`.

2. **Interpretation**: Interpret φ within the class C. The class C consists of frames or models that satisfy certain properties relevant to the Hilbert system.

3. **Induction on the Derivation**: Use induction on the number of steps in the derivation of φ within the Hilbert system.
   - **Base Case**: If φ is an axiom or an assumption, then by definition, it holds in the class C.
   - **Inductive Step**: For each rule of inference applied in the derivation, show that if the premises hold in C, then the conclusion also holds in C.
     - **Implication Introduction**: If φ is derived as `A → B`, then assume A holds in some frame, and show that B must also hold in that frame.
     - **Implication Elimination**: If φ involves implications, systematically examine each case to ensure the conditions lead to the desired conclusion.
     - **Contraposition**: Handle cases where contradiction is used to establish the validity of φ.

4. **Handling Cases**:
   - If φ is an atomic formula, rely on the axioms `axiomK` to validate it within C.
   - If φ involves disjunctions, break it down into disjunctive cases and handle each separately.
   - For negations, use the elimination rules to derive the necessary conditions.

5. **Application of Additional Rules**:
   - Use the system's specific rules (`mdd`, `nec`, `maxm`) to manage modal or generalized implications within φ.
   - For `mdd` (maximum modulus or depth), ensure that no contradictions arise from the depth-related constraints.
   - For `nec` (necessitation), if applicable, derive the necessary conditions from the premises.

6. **Conclusion**: After systematically applying these steps, conclude that under all interpretations within the class C, the formula φ holds true.

informal_statement: If the class \( C \) is determined by \( Ax \), then the finite restriction of \( FC \) is also determined by \( Ax \).
informal_proof:
To establish that the finite restriction of \( FC \) is determined by \( Ax \), we begin by acknowledging the given condition that \( C \) is determined by \( Ax \). This implies that all elements within \( C \) satisfy the properties encapsulated by \( Ax \).

Given the equality \( FC = C.\text{restrictFinite} \), we substitute \( FC \) with its finite restriction. Since \( FC \) is restricted to finite cases, we infer that \( FC \) now only includes those elements that satisfy \( C \).

By applying the lemma \( \text{FiniteFrameClass.definedBy\_of\_definedBy\_frameclass\_aux} \) with the initial condition \( h : C.\text{DefinedBy}\ Ax \), we directly obtain the conclusion. informal_proof:
We aim to prove that for any class \( C \), if \( C \) is defined by a set of axioms \( Ax \), then the finite restriction of \( C \) is also defined by \( Ax \).

**Forward Implication:**
Assume \( C \) is defined by \( Ax \). For any instance \( F \) of \( C \), we need to show that \( F \) belongs to the finite restriction of \( C \). By the definition of being defined by \( Ax \), we can apply \( Ax \) to \( F \) and by the property of finite restriction, this preserves the definition. Hence, \( F \) is in the finite restriction of \( C \).

**Reverse Implication:**
Conversely, assume that \( F \) belongs to the finite restriction of \( C \). Since \( F \) is a finite instance of \( C \), and \( C \) is defined by \( Ax \), \( Ax \) must hold for \( F \). Therefore, \( F \) is defined by \( Ax \), completing the proof.

Thus, we have shown that the finite restriction preserves the definition given by \( Ax \).

informal_statement: A finite Kripke frame class \( C \) is defined by a theory \( T \) in the natural numbers if and only if every finite frame \( F \) belongs to \( C \) precisely when \( F \) satisfies the bounded theory of \( T \) up to the top element, \( T^{\Box} \).
informal_proof:
To establish the equivalence, we consider an arbitrary finite frame \( F \) and show that \( F \in C \) if and only if \( F \vDash* T^{\Box} \).

1. **Forward Direction (\( \Rightarrow \))**: Assume \( F \in C \). By the definition of \( C \)-defined by \( T \), this means that \( F \) satisfies \( F \tFilmBox T \), i.e., \( F \vDash* T^{\Box} \).

2. **Reverse Direction (\( \Leftarrow \))**: Assume \( F \vDash* T^{\Box} \). Since \( C \) is defined by \( T \), \( F \in C \) if and only if \( F \vDash* T^{\Box} \). Therefore, \( F \in C \).

Thus, \( F \in C \) if and only if \( F \vDash* T^{\Box} \), completing the proof.

C1_dependencies.name: rfl
C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

informal_statement:
**

If there exists a finite Kripke frame in which a formula φ is not valid, then φ is not valid on the class of all finite frames.
informal_proof:
**

Suppose there exists at least one finite Kripke frame F where the formula φ is not valid. By definition, validity on a class of frames requires that φ be valid in every frame within that class. Since φ is not valid in frame F, which is a member of the class of finite frames FC, φ cannot be valid across the entire class FC. Therefore, if φ fails to be valid in any finite frame, it cannot be valid on the class of finite frames.

informal_statement: If a class $C$ of Kripke frames interprets the formula $\phi$ such that $\phi$ is valid in $C$, then for every frame in $C$, $\phi$ is valid. Conversely, if $\phi$ is valid in $C$, then $C$ models $\phi$.
informal_proof:
First, we consider the forward direction. Assume that $C \models \phi$. By definition, this means that every frame in $C$ satisfies $\phi$. Therefore, $\phi$ is valid in $C$.

For the reverse direction, assume that $\phi$ is valid in $C$. This implies that every frame in $C$ satisfies $\phi$. Hence, by definition, $C \models \phi$.

Thus, we have shown both directions of the equivalence, completing the proof.

informal_statement: For any function \( F \) and elements \( x \) and \( y \), if \( x \) and \( y \) are equal, then \( F(x) \) and \( F(y) \) are also equal.
informal_proof:
Consider arbitrary functions \( F \), and arbitrary elements \( x \) and \( y \). Assume that \( x \) and \( y \) are equal, i.e., \( x = y \). 

By substituting \( y \) with \( x \) (since they are equal), we have:
\[ F(x) = F(x) \]
This substitution does not change the truth value of the expression because \( F(x) \) and \( F(y) \) are the same when \( x = y \). 

Thus, the property holds, and we conclude that \( F(x) = F(y) \) whenever \( x = y \).

import Foundation.Vorspiel.RelItr
import Foundation.Logic.System
import Foundation.Modal.Formula
import Foundation.Modal.Hilbert.Systems

namespace LO.Modal

open System


namespace Kripke

structure Frame where
  World : Type
  Rel : Rel World World
  [world_nonempty : Nonempty World]

instance : CoeSort Frame (Type) := ⟨Frame.World⟩
instance : CoeFun Frame (λ F => F.World → F.World → Prop) := ⟨Frame.Rel⟩
instance {F : Frame} : Nonempty F.World := F.world_nonempty

abbrev Frame.Rel' {F : Frame} (x y : F.World) := F.Rel x y
infix:45 " ≺ " => Frame.Rel'

protected abbrev Frame.RelItr' {F : Frame} (n : ℕ) := F.Rel.iterate n
notation x:45 " ≺^[" n "] " y:46 => Frame.RelItr' n x y


structure FiniteFrame extends Frame where
  [world_finite : Finite toFrame.World]
instance {F : FiniteFrame} : Finite F.World := F.world_finite

def Frame.toFinite (F : Frame) [Finite F.World] : FiniteFrame where
  toFrame := F


abbrev reflexivePointFrame : FiniteFrame where
  World := Unit
  Rel := fun _ _ => True

abbrev irreflexivePointFrame : FiniteFrame where
  World := Unit
  Rel := fun _ _ => False


abbrev FrameClass := Set Frame

abbrev FiniteFrameClass := Set FiniteFrame

def FrameClass.restrictFinite (C : FrameClass) : FiniteFrameClass := { F : FiniteFrame | F.toFrame ∈ C }

def FiniteFrameClass.toFrameClass (C : FiniteFrameClass) : FrameClass := C.image (·.toFrame)

instance : Coe (FiniteFrameClass) (FrameClass) := ⟨FiniteFrameClass.toFrameClass⟩


section

abbrev AllFrameClass : FrameClass := Set.univ

abbrev AllFiniteFrameClass : FiniteFrameClass := Set.univ

end


abbrev Valuation (F : Frame) := F.World → ℕ → Prop

structure Model extends Frame where
  Val : Valuation toFrame
instance : CoeFun (Model) (λ M => M.World → ℕ → Prop) := ⟨fun m => m.Val⟩

end Kripke



namespace Formula.Kripke

def Satisfies (M : Kripke.Model) (x : M.World) : Formula ℕ → Prop
  | atom a  => M x a
  | ⊥  => False
  | φ ➝ ψ => (Satisfies M x φ) ➝ (Satisfies M x ψ)
  | □φ   => ∀ y, x ≺ y → (Satisfies M y φ)

namespace Satisfies

protected instance semantics {M : Kripke.Model} : Semantics (Formula ℕ) (M.World) := ⟨fun x ↦ Formula.Kripke.Satisfies M x⟩

variable {M : Kripke.Model} {x : M.World} {φ ψ : Formula ℕ}

@[simp] protected lemma iff_models : x ⊧ φ ↔ Kripke.Satisfies M x φ := iff_of_eq rfl

@[simp] lemma atom_def : x ⊧ atom a ↔ M x a := by simp [Satisfies];

lemma box_def : x ⊧ □φ ↔ ∀ y, x ≺ y → y ⊧ φ := by simp [Kripke.Satisfies];

lemma dia_def : x ⊧ ◇φ ↔ ∃ y, x ≺ y ∧ y ⊧ φ := by simp [Kripke.Satisfies];

lemma not_def : x ⊧ ∼φ ↔ ¬(x ⊧ φ) := by
  induction φ using Formula.rec' generalizing x with
  | _ => simp_all [Satisfies];

lemma imp_def : x ⊧ φ ➝ ψ ↔ (x ⊧ φ) → (x ⊧ ψ) := by tauto;

lemma or_def : x ⊧ φ ⋎ ψ ↔ x ⊧ φ ∨ x ⊧ ψ := by simp [Satisfies]; tauto;

lemma and_def : x ⊧ φ ⋏ ψ ↔ x ⊧ φ ∧ x ⊧ ψ := by simp [Satisfies];

lemma top_def : x ⊧ ⊤ := by simp [Satisfies];

lemma bot_def : ¬x ⊧ ⊥ := by simp [Satisfies];

protected instance : Semantics.Tarski (M.World) where
  realize_top := λ _ => top_def;
  realize_bot := λ _ => bot_def;
  realize_imp := imp_def;
  realize_not := not_def;
  realize_or := or_def;
  realize_and := and_def;

lemma negneg_def : x ⊧ ∼∼φ ↔ x ⊧ φ := by simp [Satisfies];

lemma multibox_def : x ⊧ □^[n]φ ↔ ∀ {y}, x ≺^[n] y → y ⊧ φ := by
  exact?

informal_statement: In any scenario or interpretation (referred to as a model), if implication φ implies ψ holds, then the contrapositive of that implication (which is "if not ψ then not φ") also holds in the same scenario or interpretation.
informal_proof:
Suppose we have two propositions, φ and ψ, and a model V. If in this model, φ implies ψ is true, then the contrapositive of this implication, which is "if not ψ then not φ", must also be true in the same model. This is because the contrapositive of an implication is logically equivalent to the original implication. 

To illustrate this, let's consider an example: Suppose in a given scenario, the proposition φ is "It is raining," and the proposition ψ is "The ground is wet." If φ implies ψ is true in this scenario, meaning that whenever it is raining, the ground is wet, then the contrapositive, "if the ground is not wet, then it is not raining," must also be true. This is because if the ground were wet only when it rained, then if the ground isn't wet, it couldn't have rained. Thus, both the original implication and its contrapositive hold true in the same scenario.

This logical equivalence is fundamental in formal logic and is the basis for the elimination of contraposition, which allows us to infer the contrapositive of an implication from the implication itself without any additional proof. Hence, in any model V, if φ implies ψ, then its contrapositive also holds true in V.

import Foundation.Vorspiel.RelItr

namespace LO.Modal

open System


namespace Kripke

structure Frame where
  World : Type
  Rel : Rel World World
  [world_nonempty : Nonempty World]

instance : CoeSort Frame (Type) := ⟨Frame.World⟩
instance : CoeFun Frame (λ F => F.World → F.World → Prop) := ⟨Frame.Rel⟩
instance {F : Frame} : Nonempty F.World := F.world_nonempty

abbrev Frame.Rel' {F : Frame} (x y : F.World) := F.Rel x y
infix:45 " ≺ " => Frame.Rel'

protected abbrev Frame.RelItr' {F : Frame} (n : ℕ) := F.Rel.iterate n
notation x:45 " ≺^[" n "] " y:46 => Frame.RelItr' n x y


structure FiniteFrame extends Frame where
  [world_finite : Finite toFrame.World]
instance {F : FiniteFrame} : Finite F.World := F.world_finite

def Frame.toFinite (F : Frame) [Finite F.World] : FiniteFrame where
  toFrame := F


abbrev reflexivePointFrame : FiniteFrame where
  World := Unit
  Rel := fun _ _ => True

abbrev irreflexivePointFrame : FiniteFrame where
  World := Unit
  Rel := fun _ _ => False


abbrev FrameClass := Set Frame

abbrev FiniteFrameClass := Set FiniteFrame

def FrameClass.restrictFinite (C : FrameClass) : FiniteFrameClass := { F : FiniteFrame | F.toFrame ∈ C }

def FiniteFrameClass.toFrameClass (C : FiniteFrameClass) : FrameClass := C.image (·.toFrame)

instance : Coe (FiniteFrameClass) (FrameClass) := ⟨FiniteFrameClass.toFrameClass⟩


section

abbrev AllFrameClass : FrameClass := Set.univ

abbrev AllFiniteFrameClass : FiniteFrameClass := Set.univ

end


abbrev Valuation (F : Frame) := F.World → ℕ → Prop

structure Model extends Frame where
  Val : Valuation toFrame
instance : CoeFun (Model) (λ M => M.World → ℕ → Prop) := ⟨fun m => m.Val⟩

end Kripke



namespace Formula.Kripke

def Satisfies (M : Kripke.Model) (x : M.World) : Formula ℕ → Prop
  | atom a  => M x a
  | ⊥  => False
  | φ ➝ ψ => (Satisfies M x φ) ➝ (Satisfies M x ψ)
  | □φ   => ∀ y, x ≺ y → (Satisfies M y φ)

namespace Satisfies

protected instance semantics {M : Kripke.Model} : Semantics (Formula ℕ) (M.World) := ⟨fun x ↦ Formula.Kripke.Satisfies M x⟩

variable {M : Kripke.Model} {x : M.World} {φ ψ : Formula ℕ}

@[simp] protected lemma iff_models : x ⊧ φ ↔ Kripke.Satisfies M x φ := iff_of_eq rfl

@[simp] lemma atom_def : x ⊧ atom a ↔ M x a := by simp [Satisfies];

lemma box_def : x ⊧ □φ ↔ ∀ y, x ≺ y → y ⊧ φ := by simp [Kripke.Satisfies];

lemma dia_def : x ⊧ ◇φ ↔ ∃ y, x ≺ y ∧ y ⊧ φ := by simp [Kripke.Satisfies];

lemma not_def : x ⊧ ∼φ ↔ ¬(x ⊧ φ) := by
  induction φ using Formula.rec' generalizing x with
  | _ => simp_all [Satisfies];

lemma imp_def : x ⊧ φ ➝ ψ ↔ (x ⊧ φ) → (x ⊧ ψ) := by tauto;

lemma or_def : x ⊧ φ ⋎ ψ ↔ x ⊧ φ ∨ x ⊧ ψ := by simp [Satisfies]; tauto;

lemma and_def : x ⊧ φ ⋏ ψ ↔ x ⊧ φ ∧ x ⊧ ψ := by simp [Satisfies];

lemma top_def : x ⊧ ⊤ := by simp [Satisfies];

lemma bot_def : ¬x ⊧ ⊥ := by simp [Satisfies];

protected instance : Semantics.Tarski (M.World) where
  realize_top := by exact?

informal_statement: In the context of a model \( F \) and a valuation \( V \), the implication \( \phi \rightarrow \psi \) is valid. This means that whenever \( \phi \) holds under \( V \), \( \psi \) must also hold under \( V \) within the model \( F \).
informal_proof:
To prove that \( \phi \rightarrow \psi \) is valid over the model \( F \) with respect to the valuation \( V \), we can utilize the formal lemma `ValidOnModel.imply₁`. According to this lemma, we have:

\[
F \models (\text{Axioms.Imply} \; \phi \; \psi)
\]

This directly implies that for all valuations \( V \), the validity of the implication \( \phi \rightarrow \psi \) holds in \( F \) under \( V \). Therefore, by invoking `ValidOnModel.imply₁` with \( F \) and \( V \) as parameters, we confirm that \( \phi \rightarrow \psi \) is indeed valid within the specified model and valuation.

import Foundation.Vorspiel.RelItr
import Foundation.Logic.System
import Foundation.Modal.Formula
import Foundation.Modal.Hilbert.Systems

namespace LO.Modal

open System


namespace Kripke

structure Frame where
  World : Type
  Rel : Rel World World
  [world_nonempty : Nonempty World]

instance : CoeSort Frame (Type) := ⟨Frame.World⟩
instance : CoeFun Frame (λ F => F.World → F.World → Prop) := ⟨Frame.Rel⟩
instance {F : Frame} : Nonempty F.World := F.world_nonempty

abbrev Frame.Rel' {F : Frame} (x y : F.World) := F.Rel x y
infix:45 " ≺ " => Frame.Rel'

protected abbrev Frame.RelItr' {F : Frame} (n : ℕ) := F.Rel.iterate n
notation x:45 " ≺^[" n "] " y:46 => Frame.RelItr' n x y


structure FiniteFrame extends Frame where
  [world_finite : Finite toFrame.World]
instance {F : FiniteFrame} : Finite F.World := F.world_finite

def Frame.toFinite (F : Frame) [Finite F.World] : FiniteFrame where
  toFrame := F


abbrev reflexivePointFrame : FiniteFrame where
  World := Unit
  Rel := fun _ _ => True

abbrev irreflexivePointFrame : FiniteFrame where
  World := Unit
  Rel := fun _ _ => False


abbrev FrameClass := Set Frame

abbrev FiniteFrameClass := Set FiniteFrame

def FrameClass.restrictFinite (C : FrameClass) : FiniteFrameClass := { F : FiniteFrame | F.toFrame ∈ C }

def FiniteFrameClass.toFrameClass (C : FiniteFrameClass) : FrameClass := C.image (·.toFrame)

instance : Coe (FiniteFrameClass) (FrameClass) := ⟨FiniteFrameClass.toFrameClass⟩


section

abbrev AllFrameClass : FrameClass := Set.univ

abbrev AllFiniteFrameClass : FiniteFrameClass := Set.univ

end


abbrev Valuation (F : Frame) := F.World → ℕ → Prop

structure Model extends Frame where
  Val : Valuation toFrame
instance : CoeFun (Model) (λ M => M.World → ℕ → Prop) := ⟨fun m => m.Val⟩

end Kripke



namespace Formula.Kripke

def Satisfies (M : Kripke.Model) (x : M.World) : Formula ℕ → Prop
  | atom a  => M x a
  | ⊥  => False
  | φ ➝ ψ => (Satisfies M x φ) ➝ (Satisfies M x ψ)
  | □φ   => ∀ y, x ≺ y → (Satisfies M y φ)

namespace Satisfies

protected instance semantics {M : Kripke.Model} : Semantics (Formula ℕ) (M.World) := ⟨fun x ↦ Formula.Kripke.Satisfies M x⟩

variable {M : Kripke.Model} {x : M.World} {φ ψ : Formula ℕ}

@[simp] protected lemma iff_models : x ⊧ φ ↔ Kripke.Satisfies M x φ := iff_of_eq rfl

@[simp] lemma atom_def : x ⊧ atom a ↔ M x a := by simp [Satisfies];

lemma box_def : x ⊧ □φ ↔ ∀ y, x ≺ y → y ⊧ φ := by simp [Kripke.Satisfies];

lemma dia_def : x ⊧ ◇φ ↔ ∃ y, x ≺ y ∧ y ⊧ φ := by simp [Kripke.Satisfies];

lemma not_def : x ⊧ ∼φ ↔ ¬(x ⊧ φ) := by
  induction φ using Formula.rec' generalizing x with
  | _ => simp_all [Satisfies];

lemma imp_def : x ⊧ φ ➝ ψ ↔ (x ⊧ φ) → (x ⊧ ψ) := by tauto;

lemma or_def : x ⊧ φ ⋎ ψ ↔ x ⊧ φ ∨ x ⊧ ψ := by simp [Satisfies]; tauto;

lemma and_def : x ⊧ φ ⋏ ψ ↔ x ⊧ φ ∧ x ⊧ ψ := by simp [Satisfies];

lemma top_def : x ⊧ ⊤ := by simp [Satisfies];

import Foundation.Vorspiel.RelItr
import Foundation.Logic.System
import Foundation.Modal.Formula
import Foundation.Modal.Hilbert.Systems

namespace LO.Modal

open System


namespace Kripke

structure Frame where
  World : Type
  Rel : Rel World World
  [world_nonempty : Nonempty World]

instance : CoeSort Frame (Type) := ⟨Frame.World⟩
instance : CoeFun Frame (λ F => F.World → F.World → Prop) := ⟨Frame.Rel⟩
instance {F : Frame} : Nonempty F.World := F.world_nonempty

abbrev Frame.Rel' {F : Frame} (x y : F.World) := F.Rel x y
infix:45 " ≺ " => Frame.Rel'

protected abbrev Frame.RelItr' {F : Frame} (n : ℕ) := F.Rel.iterate n
notation x:45 " ≺^[" n "] " y:46 => Frame.RelItr' n x y


structure FiniteFrame extends Frame where
  [world_finite : Finite toFrame.World]
instance {F : FiniteFrame} : Finite F.World := F.world_finite

def Frame.toFinite (F : Frame) [Finite F.World] : FiniteFrame where
  toFrame := F


abbrev reflexivePointFrame : FiniteFrame where
  World := Unit
  Rel := fun _ _ => True

abbrev irreflexivePointFrame : FiniteFrame where
  World := Unit
  Rel := fun _ _ => False


abbrev FrameClass := Set Frame

abbrev FiniteFrameClass := Set FiniteFrame

def FrameClass.restrictFinite (C : FrameClass) : FiniteFrameClass := { F : FiniteFrame | F.toFrame ∈ C }

def FiniteFrameClass.toFrameClass (C : FiniteFrameClass) : FrameClass := C.image (·.toFrame)

instance : Coe (FiniteFrameClass) (FrameClass) := ⟨FiniteFrameClass.toFrameClass⟩


section

abbrev AllFrameClass : FrameClass := Set.univ

abbrev AllFiniteFrameClass : FiniteFrameClass := Set.univ

end


abbrev Valuation (F : Frame) := F.World → ℕ → Prop

structure Model extends Frame where
  Val : Valuation toFrame
instance : CoeFun (Model) (λ M => M.World → ℕ → Prop) := ⟨fun m => m.Val⟩

end Kripke



namespace Formula.Kripke

def Satisfies (M : Kripke.Model) (x : M.World) : Formula ℕ → Prop
  | atom a  => M x a
  | ⊥  => False
  | φ ➝ ψ => (Satisfies M x φ) ➝ (Satisfies M x ψ)
  | □φ   => ∀ y, x ≺ y → (Satisfies M y φ)

namespace Satisfies

protected instance semantics {M : Kripke.Model} : Semantics (Formula ℕ) (M.World) := ⟨fun x ↦ Formula.Kripke.Satisfies M x⟩

variable {M : Kripke.Model} {x : M.World} {φ ψ : Formula ℕ}

@[simp] protected lemma iff_models : x ⊧ φ ↔ Kripke.Satisfies M x φ := iff_of_eq rfl

@[simp] lemma atom_def : x ⊧ atom a ↔ M x a := by simp [Satisfies];

lemma box_def : x ⊧ □φ ↔ ∀ y, x ≺ y → y ⊧ φ := by simp [Kripke.Satisfies];

lemma dia_def : x ⊧ ◇φ ↔ ∃ y, x ≺ y ∧ y ⊧ φ := by simp [Kripke.Satisfies];

lemma not_def : x ⊧ ∼φ ↔ ¬(x ⊧ φ) := by
  induction φ using Formula.rec' generalizing x with
  | _ => simp_all [Satisfies];

lemma imp_def : x ⊧ φ ➝ ψ ↔ (x ⊧ φ) → (x ⊧ ψ) := by tauto;

lemma or_def : x ⊧ φ ⋎ ψ ↔ x ⊧ φ ∨ x ⊧ ψ := by simp [Satisfies]; tauto;

lemma and_def : x ⊧ φ ⋏ ψ ↔ x ⊧ φ ∧ x ⊧ ψ := by simp [Satisfies];

lemma top_def : x ⊧ ⊤ := by exact?

If from a certain set of assumptions \( F \), assuming \( \varphi \) leads to \( \psi \), and \( \varphi \) is true under \( F \), then \( \psi \) must also be true under \( F \).

</STATEMENT>
<PROOF>

To prove the lemma `mdp`, we start by assuming that from a set of assumptions \( F \), assuming \( \varphi \) leads to \( \psi \) (i.e., \( F \vdash \varphi \rightarrow \psi \)) and that \( \varphi \) is true under \( F \) (i.e., \( F \vdash \varphi \)). 

We consider an arbitrary model \( V \) where \( F \) holds. Under \( V \), since \( F \vdash \varphi \rightarrow \psi \), if \( \varphi \) is true under \( V \), then \( \psi \) must also be true under \( V \). This follows directly from the definition of logical consequence. 

Therefore, under all models \( V \) where \( F \) holds, \( \psi \) must be true whenever \( \varphi \) is true. This establishes that \( F \vdash \psi \).

import Foundation.Vorspiel.RelItr
import Foundation.Logic.System
import Foundation.Modal.Formula
import Foundation.Modal.Hilbert.Systems

namespace LO.Modal

open System


namespace Kripke

structure Frame where
  World : Type
  Rel : Rel World World
  [world_nonempty : Nonempty World]

instance : CoeSort Frame (Type) := ⟨Frame.World⟩
instance : CoeFun Frame (λ F => F.World → F.World → Prop) := ⟨Frame.Rel⟩
instance {F : Frame} : Nonempty F.World := F.world_nonempty

abbrev Frame.Rel' {F : Frame} (x y : F.World) := F.Rel x y
infix:45 " ≺ " => Frame.Rel'

protected abbrev Frame.RelItr' {F : Frame} (n : ℕ) := F.Rel.iterate n
notation x:45 " ≺^[" n "] " y:46 => Frame.RelItr' n x y


structure FiniteFrame extends Frame where
  [world_finite : Finite toFrame.World]
instance {F : FiniteFrame} : Finite F.World := F.world_finite

def Frame.toFinite (F : Frame) [Finite F.World] : FiniteFrame where
  toFrame := F


abbrev reflexivePointFrame : FiniteFrame where
  World := Unit
  Rel := fun _ _ => True

abbrev irreflexivePointFrame : FiniteFrame where
  World := Unit
  Rel := fun _ _ => False


abbrev FrameClass := Set Frame

abbrev FiniteFrameClass := Set FiniteFrame

def FrameClass.restrictFinite (C : FrameClass) : FiniteFrameClass := { F : FiniteFrame | F.toFrame ∈ C }

def FiniteFrameClass.toFrameClass (C : FiniteFrameClass) : FrameClass := C.image (·.toFrame)

instance : Coe (FiniteFrameClass) (FrameClass) := ⟨FiniteFrameClass.toFrameClass⟩


section

abbrev AllFrameClass : FrameClass := Set.univ

abbrev AllFiniteFrameClass : FiniteFrameClass := Set.univ

end


abbrev Valuation (F : Frame) := F.World → ℕ → Prop

structure Model extends Frame where
  Val : Valuation toFrame
instance : CoeFun (Model) (λ M => M.World → ℕ → Prop) := ⟨fun m => m.Val⟩

end Kripke



namespace Formula.Kripke

def Satisfies (M : Kripke.Model) (x : M.World) : Formula ℕ → Prop
  | atom a  => M x a
  | ⊥  => False
  | φ ➝ ψ => (Satisfies M x φ) ➝ (Satisfies M x ψ)
  | □φ   => ∀ y, x ≺ y → (Satisfies M y φ)

namespace Satisfies

protected instance semantics {M : Kripke.Model} : Semantics (Formula ℕ) (M.World) := ⟨fun x ↦ Formula.Kripke.Satisfies M x⟩

variable {M : Kripke.Model} {x : M.World} {φ ψ : Formula ℕ}

@[simp] protected lemma iff_models : x ⊧ φ ↔ Kripke.Satisfies M x φ := iff_of_eq rfl

@[simp] lemma atom_def : x ⊧ atom a ↔ M x a := by simp [Satisfies];

lemma box_def : x ⊧ □φ ↔ ∀ y, x ≺ y → y ⊧ φ := by simp [Kripke.Satisfies];

lemma dia_def : x ⊧ ◇φ ↔ ∃ y, x ≺ y ∧ y ⊧ φ := by simp [Kripke.Satisfies];

lemma not_def : x ⊧ ∼φ ↔ ¬(x ⊧ φ) := by
  induction φ using Formula.rec' generalizing x with
  | _ => simp_all [Satisfies];

lemma imp_def : x ⊧ φ ➝ ψ ↔ (x ⊧ φ) → (x ⊧ ψ) := by tauto;

lemma or_def : x ⊧ φ ⋎ ψ ↔ x ⊧ φ ∨ x ⊧ ψ := by simp [Satisfies]; tauto;

lemma and_def : x ⊧ φ ⋏ ψ ↔ x ⊧ φ ∧ x ⊧ ψ := by exact?

namespace LO.Modal

open System


namespace Kripke

structure Frame where
  World : Type
  Rel : Rel World World
  [world_nonempty : Nonempty World]

instance : CoeSort Frame (Type) := ⟨Frame.World⟩
instance : CoeFun Frame (λ F => F.World → F.World → Prop) := ⟨Frame.Rel⟩
instance {F : Frame} : Nonempty F.World := F.world_nonempty

abbrev Frame.Rel' {F : Frame} (x y : F.World) := F.Rel x y

protected abbrev Frame.RelItr' {F : Frame} (n : ℕ) := F.Rel.iterate n
notation x:45 " ≺^[" n "] " y:46 => Frame.RelItr' n x y


structure FiniteFrame extends Frame where
  [world_finite : Finite toFrame.World]
instance {F : FiniteFrame} : Finite F.World := F.world_finite

def Frame.toFinite (F : Frame) [Finite F.World] : FiniteFrame where
  toFrame := F


abbrev reflexivePointFrame : FiniteFrame where
  World := Unit
  Rel := fun _ _ => True

abbrev irreflexivePointFrame : FiniteFrame where
  World := Unit
  Rel := fun _ _ => False


abbrev FrameClass := Set Frame

abbrev FiniteFrameClass := Set FiniteFrame

def FrameClass.restrictFinite (C : FrameClass) : FiniteFrameClass := { F : FiniteFrame | F.toFrame ∈ C }

def FiniteFrameClass.toFrameClass (C : FiniteFrameClass) : FrameClass := C.image (·.toFrame)

instance : Coe (FiniteFrameClass) (FrameClass) := ⟨FiniteFrameClass.toFrameClass⟩


section

abbrev AllFrameClass : FrameClass := Set.univ

abbrev AllFiniteFrameClass : FiniteFrameClass := Set.univ

end


abbrev Valuation (F : Frame) := F.World → ℕ → Prop

structure Model extends Frame where
  Val : Valuation toFrame
instance : CoeFun (Model) (λ M => M.World → ℕ → Prop) := ⟨fun m => m.Val⟩

end Kripke



namespace Formula.Kripke

def Satisfies (M : Kripke.Model) (x : M.World) : Formula ℕ → Prop
  | atom a  => M x a
  | ⊥  => False
  | φ ➝ ψ => (Satisfies M x φ) ➝ (Satisfies M x ψ)
  | □φ   => ∀ y, x ≺ y → (Satisfies M y φ)

namespace Satisfies

protected instance semantics {M : Kripke.Model} : Semantics (Formula ℕ) (M.World) := ⟨fun x ↦ Formula.Kripke.Satisfies M x⟩

variable {M : Kripke.Model} {x : M.World} {φ ψ : Formula ℕ}

@[simp] protected lemma iff_models : x ⊧ φ ↔ Kripke.Satisfies M x φ := iff_of_eq rfl

@[simp] lemma atom_def : x ⊧ atom a ↔ M x a := by simp [Satisfies];

lemma box_def : x ⊧ □φ ↔ ∀ y, x ≺ y → y ⊧ φ := by simp [Kripke.Satisfies];

lemma dia_def : x ⊧ ◇φ ↔ ∃ y, x ≺ y ∧ y ⊧ φ := by simp [Kripke.Satisfies];

lemma not_def : x ⊧ ∼φ ↔ ¬(x ⊧ φ) := by
  induction φ using Formula.rec' generalizing x with
  | _ => simp_all [Satisfies];

lemma imp_def : x ⊧ φ ➝ ψ ↔ (x ⊧ φ) → (x ⊧ ψ) := by tauto;

lemma or_def : x ⊧ φ ⋎ ψ ↔ x ⊧ φ ∨ x ⊧ ψ := by exact?

structure Frame where

  [world_nonempty : Nonempty World]

instance : CoeFun Frame (λ F => F.World → F.World → Prop) := ⟨Frame.Rel⟩
instance {F : Frame} : Nonempty F.World := F.world_nonempty

  toFrame := F

instance : Coe (FiniteFrameClass) (FrameClass) := ⟨FiniteFrameClass.toFrameClass⟩


section

abbrev AllFiniteFrameClass : FiniteFrameClass := Set.univ

end


abbrev Valuation (F : Frame) := F.World → ℕ → Prop

def Satisfies (M : Kripke.Model) (x : M.World) : Formula ℕ → Prop
  | atom a  => M x a
  | ⊥  => False
  | φ ➝ ψ => (Satisfies M x φ) ➝ (Satisfies M x ψ)
  | □φ   => ∀ y, x ≺ y → (Satisfies M y φ)

@[simp] protected lemma iff_models : x ⊧ φ ↔ Kripke.Satisfies M x φ := iff_of_eq rfl

lemma box_def : x ⊧ □φ ↔ ∀ y, x ≺ y → y ⊧ φ := by simp [Kripke.Satisfies];

informal_statement: A set of instance statements Φ* is equivalent to the set of statements Φ such that every φ in Φ is provable from the theory F.
informal_proof: By definition, a theory F semantically entails a set of instance statements Φ* if and only if every φ in Φ* is provable from F. This directly follows from the fundamental principle that Φ* contains exactly those statements that can be derived using the rules of inference of F. Therefore, the equivalence holds because both directions are inherently linked through the semantics of the theory and its instances.

import Foundation.Vorspiel.RelItr
import Foundation.Logic.System
import Foundation.Modal.Formula
import Foundation.Modal.Hilbert.Systems

namespace LO.Modal

open System


namespace Kripke

structure Frame where
  World : Type
  Rel : Rel World World
  [world_nonempty : Nonempty World]

instance : CoeSort Frame (Type) := ⟨Frame.World⟩
instance : CoeFun Frame (λ F => F.World → F.World → Prop) := ⟨Frame.Rel⟩
instance {F : Frame} : Nonempty F.World := F.world_nonempty

abbrev Frame.Rel' {F : Frame} (x y : F.World) := F.Rel x y
infix:45 " ≺ " => Frame.Rel'

protected abbrev Frame.RelItr' {F : Frame} (n : ℕ) := F.Rel.iterate n
notation x:45 " ≺^[" n "] " y:46 => Frame.RelItr' n x y


structure FiniteFrame extends Frame where
  [world_finite : Finite toFrame.World]
instance {F : FiniteFrame} : Finite F.World := F.world_finite

def Frame.toFinite (F : Frame) [Finite F.World] : FiniteFrame where
  toFrame := F


abbrev reflexivePointFrame : FiniteFrame where
  World := Unit
  Rel := fun _ _ => True

abbrev irreflexivePointFrame : FiniteFrame where
  World := Unit
  Rel := fun _ _ => False


abbrev FrameClass := Set Frame

abbrev FiniteFrameClass := Set FiniteFrame

def FrameClass.restrictFinite (C : FrameClass) : FiniteFrameClass := { F : FiniteFrame | F.toFrame ∈ C }

def FiniteFrameClass.toFrameClass (C : FiniteFrameClass) : FrameClass := C.image (·.toFrame)

instance : Coe (FiniteFrameClass) (FrameClass) := ⟨FiniteFrameClass.toFrameClass⟩


section

abbrev AllFrameClass : FrameClass := Set.univ

abbrev AllFiniteFrameClass : FiniteFrameClass := Set.univ

end


abbrev Valuation (F : Frame) := F.World → ℕ → Prop

structure Model extends Frame where
  Val : Valuation toFrame
instance : CoeFun (Model) (λ M => M.World → ℕ → Prop) := ⟨fun m => m.Val⟩

end Kripke



namespace Formula.Kripke

def Satisfies (M : Kripke.Model) (x : M.World) : Formula ℕ → Prop
  | atom a  => M x a
  | ⊥  => False
  | φ ➝ ψ => (Satisfies M x φ) ➝ (Satisfies M x ψ)
  | □φ   => ∀ y, x ≺ y → (Satisfies M y φ)

namespace Satisfies

protected instance semantics {M : Kripke.Model} : Semantics (Formula ℕ) (M.World) := ⟨fun x ↦ Formula.Kripke.Satisfies M x⟩

variable {M : Kripke.Model} {x : M.World} {φ ψ : Formula ℕ}

@[simp] protected lemma iff_models : x ⊧ φ ↔ Kripke.Satisfies M x φ := iff_of_eq rfl

@[simp] lemma atom_def : x ⊧ atom a ↔ M x a := by simp [Satisfies];

lemma box_def : x ⊧ □φ ↔ ∀ y, x ≺ y → y ⊧ φ := by simp [Kripke.Satisfies];

lemma dia_def : x ⊧ ◇φ ↔ ∃ y, x ≺ y ∧ y ⊧ φ := by simp [Kripke.Satisfies];

lemma not_def : x ⊧ ∼φ ↔ ¬(x ⊧ φ) := by
  induction φ using Formula.rec' generalizing x with
  | _ => simp_all [Satisfies];

C1_dependencies.content:
/--
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.
-/
@[match_pattern] def rfl {α : Sort u} {a : α} : Eq a a := Eq.refl a

informal_statement: If in a model $M$, the implication $\varphi \rightarrow \psi$ is valid, then $M$ satisfies the elimination by contraction condition for $\varphi$ and $\psi$.
informal_proof:
Given that in model $M$, $\varphi \rightarrow \psi$ is valid, we aim to show that $M$ satisfies the elimination by contraction condition for $\varphi$ and $\psi$. 

In classical logic, eliminations by contraction typically allow for handling implications in proofs by retaining the necessity of certain assumptions or hypotheses. Specifically, if $\varphi \rightarrow \psi$ is valid under model $M$, this implies that whenever $\varphi$ is true, so is $\psi$, within the structure of $M$. 

The elimination by contraction process ensures that if $\varphi$ leads to $\psi$, $M$ maintains consistency by not introducing any contradictions when $\varphi$ is eliminated in favor of $\psi$. This is foundational to classical reasoning, where the ability to derive new truths from existing ones does not lead to inconsistencies.

Thus, the validity of $\varphi \rightarrow \psi$ in model $M$ inherently satisfies the elimContra condition. This condition is essential for maintaining the logical integrity and coherence of $M$ when applying classical logical principles that permit contractions and simplifications in proofs.

informal_statement: For any model $M$, if $\varphi \implies \psi$ and $\psi \implies \chi$, then $\varphi \implies \chi$.
informal_proof:
Consider an arbitrary model \( M \). Our goal is to establish that if \( \varphi \) implies \( \psi \) and \( \psi \) implies \( \chi \) within this model, then \( \varphi \) necessarily implies \( \chi \).

1. **Given Implications**: Within the model \( M \), we are provided that \( \varphi \implies \psi \) and \( \psi \implies \chi \). This means that if \( M \) satisfies \( \varphi \), it must also satisfy \( \psi \), and subsequently, if \( M \) satisfies \( \psi \), it must satisfy \( \chi \).

2. **Logical Transitivity**: In classical logic, implication is transitive. That is, if \( \varphi \implies \psi \) and \( \psi \implies \chi \) are both true, then \( \varphi \implies \chi \) must also hold. This property derives from the structural rules governing implication in logical systems.

3. **Conclusion by Deduction**: By applying the transitivity of implication, we directly infer that \( \varphi \) implies \( \chi \).

Hence, for any model \( M \), if \( \varphi \) implies \( \psi \) and \( \psi \) implies \( \chi \), then \( \varphi \) implies \( \chi \).

import Foundation.Vorspiel.RelItr
import Foundation.Logic.System
import Foundation.Modal.Formula
import Foundation.Modal.Hilbert.Systems

namespace LO.Modal

open System


namespace Kripke

structure Frame where
  World : Type
  Rel : Rel World World
  [world_nonempty : Nonempty World]

instance : CoeSort Frame (Type) := ⟨Frame.World⟩
instance : CoeFun Frame (λ F => F.World → F.World → Prop) := ⟨Frame.Rel⟩
instance {F : Frame} : Nonempty F.World := F.world_nonempty

abbrev Frame.Rel' {F : Frame} (x y : F.World) := F.Rel x y
infix:45 " ≺ " => Frame.Rel'

protected abbrev Frame.RelItr' {F : Frame} (n : ℕ) := F.Rel.iterate n
notation x:45 " ≺^[" n "] " y:46 => Frame.RelItr' n x y


structure FiniteFrame extends Frame where
  [world_finite : Finite toFrame.World]
instance {F : FiniteFrame} : Finite F.World := F.world_finite

def Frame.toFinite (F : Frame) [Finite F.World] : FiniteFrame where
  toFrame := F


abbrev reflexivePointFrame : FiniteFrame where
  World := Unit
  Rel := fun _ _ => True

abbrev irreflexivePointFrame : FiniteFrame where
  World := Unit
  Rel := fun _ _ => False


abbrev FrameClass := Set Frame

abbrev FiniteFrameClass := Set FiniteFrame

def FrameClass.restrictFinite (C : FrameClass) : FiniteFrameClass := { F : FiniteFrame | F.toFrame ∈ C }

def FiniteFrameClass.toFrameClass (C : FiniteFrameClass) : FrameClass := C.image (·.toFrame)

instance : Coe (FiniteFrameClass) (FrameClass) := ⟨FiniteFrameClass.toFrameClass⟩


section

abbrev AllFrameClass : FrameClass := Set.univ

abbrev AllFiniteFrameClass : FiniteFrameClass := Set.univ

end


abbrev Valuation (F : Frame) := F.World → ℕ → Prop

structure Model extends Frame where
  Val : Valuation toFrame
instance : CoeFun (Model) (λ M => M.World → ℕ → Prop) := ⟨fun m => m.Val⟩

end Kripke



namespace Formula.Kripke

def Satisfies (M : Kripke.Model) (x : M.World) : Formula ℕ → Prop
  | atom a  => M x a
  | ⊥  => False
  | φ ➝ ψ => (Satisfies M x φ) ➝ (Satisfies M x ψ)
  | □φ   => ∀ y, x ≺ y → (Satisfies M y φ)

informal_proof:
To understand the statement, let's break it down. The lemma is asserting a fundamental property in logic: If the axioms syntactically entail that φ implies ψ, then semantically, in any model that satisfies the axioms, φ implies ψ.

Here’s a step-by-step explanation:

1. **Understanding the Terms**:
   - **Axioms**: A set of foundational statements assumed to be true within a logical system.
   - **Imply (φ → ψ)**: A logical connective indicating that if φ is true, then ψ must also be true.
   - **Model**: A structure that assigns truth values to the propositions in the system.

2. **Formal Statement**:
   - The lemma states that if the axioms syntactically entail φ → ψ (Axioms.Imply₁ φ ψ), then any model M that satisfies the axioms will also satisfy φ → ψ.

3. **Informal Proof**:
   - **Step 1: Definition of Validity**:
     - In logic, a statement is valid if it holds true in every possible model.
     - Here, φ → ψ is valid if and only if every model M that satisfies the axioms also satisfies φ → ψ.

   - **Step 2: Applying the Lemma**:
     - Given that the axioms entail φ → ψ (Axioms-syntax), by definition, φ → ψ is a logical consequence of the axioms.
     - By completeness and soundness theorems in logic:
       - **Soundness**: If φ → ψ is syntactically entailed by the axioms, then it is semantically true in every model of the axioms.
     - Therefore, in any model M of the axioms, φ → ψ holds true.

   - **Step 3: Conclusion**:
     - Hence, if the axioms syntactically imply φ → ψ, they semantically imply it across all models M.
     - Therefore, the statement holds: If the axioms entail φ → ψ, then in any model M, φ implies ψ.

   - Formalized, M ⊧ (Axioms.Imply₁ φ ψ) means that φ → ψ is valid in model M.

import Foundation.Vorspiel.RelItr
import Foundation.Logic.System
import Foundation.Modal.Formula
import Foundation.Modal.Hilbert.Systems

namespace LO.Modal

open System


namespace Kripke

structure Frame where
  World : Type
  Rel : Rel World World
  [world_nonempty : Nonempty World]

instance : CoeSort Frame (Type) := ⟨Frame.World⟩
instance : CoeFun Frame (λ F => F.World → F.World → Prop) := ⟨Frame.Rel⟩
instance {F : Frame} : Nonempty F.World := F.world_nonempty

abbrev Frame.Rel' {F : Frame} (x y : F.World) := F.Rel x y
infix:45 " ≺ " => Frame.Rel'

structure FiniteFrame extends Frame where
  [world_finite : Finite toFrame.World]
instance {F : FiniteFrame} : Finite F.World := F.world_finite

def Frame.toFinite (F : Frame) [Finite F.World] : FiniteFrame where
  toFrame := F


abbrev reflexivePointFrame : FiniteFrame where
  World := Unit
  Rel := fun _ _ => True

abbrev irreflexivePointFrame : FiniteFrame where
  World := Unit
  Rel := fun _ _ => False


abbrev FrameClass := Set Frame

abbrev FiniteFrameClass := Set FiniteFrame

def FrameClass.restrictFinite (C : FrameClass) : FiniteFrameClass := { F : FiniteFrame | F.toFrame ∈ C }

def FiniteFrameClass.toFrameClass (C : FiniteFrameClass) : FrameClass := C.image (·.toFrame)

instance : Coe (FiniteFrameClass) (FrameClass) := ⟨FiniteFrameClass.toFrameClass⟩


section

abbrev AllFrameClass : FrameClass := Set.univ

abbrev AllFiniteFrameClass : FiniteFrameClass := Set.univ

end


abbrev Valuation (F : Frame) := F.World → ℕ → Prop

structure Model extends Frame where
  Val : Valuation toFrame

  Val : Valuation toFrame

informal_statement: If a model \( \mathcal{M} \) satisfies the implication \( \phi \rightarrow \psi \) and also satisfies \( \phi \), then \( \mathcal{M} \) necessarily satisfies \( \psi \).
informal_proof:
To establish that \( \mathcal{M} \) satisfies \( \psi \) under the given conditions, we proceed as follows:

1. **Introduction of an Arbitrary Element**: Let \( x \) be an arbitrary element in the domain of \( \mathcal{M} \).

2. **Application of the Implication**: Given that \( \mathcal{M} \models \phi \rightarrow \psi \), by definition of logical consequence, if \( \mathcal{M} \) satisfies \( \phi \) at \( x \), then \( \psi \) must also be satisfied at \( x \).

3. **Satisfaction of \( \phi \)**: From the hypothesis \( \mathcal{M} \models \phi \), it follows that \( \phi \) holds in \( \mathcal{M} \) at every element, including \( x \).

4. **Conclusion via Modus Ponens**: Combining the implications and the fact that \( \phi \) holds at \( x \), we apply the principle of modus ponens to conclude that \( \psi \) must hold at \( x \).

5. **Generalization**: Since \( x \) was arbitrary, this conclusion holds for all elements in the domain of \( \mathcal{M} \), thereby establishing that \( \mathcal{M} \models \psi \).

Therefore, the lemma is proven: If \( \mathcal{M} \models \phi \rightarrow \psi \) and \( \mathcal{M} \models \phi \), then \( \mathcal{M} \models \psi \).

informal_statement: Given any Kripke model \( M \) and a formula \( f \), the formula \( f \) is true in \( M \) (denoted \( M \vDash f \)) if and only if \( f \) is valid on \( M \) according to Kripke semantics (denoted \( \text{Kripke.ValidOnModel}(M, f) \)).
informal_proof:
We aim to establish the equivalence between the semantic truth of \( f \) in model \( M \) and its validity according to Kripke semantics on \( M \).

1. **Understanding Equivalence**: The statement \( M \vDash f \leftrightarrow \text{Kripke.ValidOnModel}(M, f) \) asserts that two definitions of validity—sematical truth in the model and validity within the Kripke framework—are equivalent.

2. **Definitional Equality**: The lemma leverages `rfl`, which in Lean4 checks for definitional equality. Here, it indicates that the two concepts of validity are defined such that they are the same in this context.

3. **Conclusion**: Given the definitional equivalence, we conclude that if \( M \vDash f \), then by `rfl`, \( \text{Kripke.ValidOnModel}(M, f) \) must hold, and vice versa. This bidirectional implication completes the proof of the equivalence.

import Foundation.Vorspiel.RelItr
import Foundation.Logic.System
import Foundation.Modal.Formula
import Foundation.Modal.Hilbert.Systems

namespace LO.Modal

open System


namespace Kripke

structure Frame where
  World : Type
  Rel : Rel World World
  [world_nonempty : Nonempty World]

instance : CoeSort Frame (Type) := ⟨Frame.World⟩
instance : CoeFun Frame (λ F => F.World → F.World → Prop) := ⟨Frame.Rel⟩
instance {F : Frame} : Nonempty F.World := F.world_nonempty

abbrev Frame.Rel' {F : Frame} (x y : F.World) := F.Rel x y
infix:45 " ≺ " => Frame.Rel'

protected abbrev Frame.RelItr' {F : Frame} (n : ℕ) := F.Rel.iterate n
notation x:45 " ≺^[" n "] " y:46 => Frame.RelItr' n x y


structure FiniteFrame extends Frame where
  [world_finite : Finite toFrame.World]
instance {F : FiniteFrame} : Finite F.World := F.world_finite

def Frame.toFinite (F : Frame) [Finite F.World] : FiniteFrame where
  toFrame := F


abbrev reflexivePointFrame : FiniteFrame where
  World := Unit
  Rel := fun _ _ => True

abbrev irreflexivePointFrame : FiniteFrame where
  World := Unit
  Rel := fun _ _ => False


abbrev FrameClass := Set Frame

abbrev FiniteFrameClass := Set FiniteFrame

def FrameClass.restrictFinite (C : FrameClass) : FiniteFrameClass := { F : FiniteFrame | F.toFrame ∈ C }

def FiniteFrameClass.toFrameClass (C : FiniteFrameClass) : FrameClass := C.image (·.toFrame)

instance : Coe (FiniteFrameClass) (FrameClass) := ⟨FiniteFrameClass.toFrameClass⟩


section

abbrev AllFrameClass : FrameClass := Set.univ

abbrev AllFiniteFrameClass : FiniteFrameClass := Set.univ

end


abbrev Valuation (F : Frame) := F.World → ℕ → Prop

structure Model extends Frame where
  Val : Valuation toFrame
annotation:
structure Model extends Frame where
  Val : Valuation toFrame

import Foundation.Vorspiel.RelItr
import Foundation.Logic.System
import Foundation.Modal.Formula
import Foundation.Modal.Hilbert.Systems

namespace LO.Modal

open System


namespace Kripke

structure Frame where
  World : Type
  Rel : Rel World World
  [world_nonempty : Nonempty World]

instance : CoeSort Frame (Type) := ⟨Frame.World⟩
instance : CoeFun Frame (λ F => F.World → F.World → Prop) := ⟨Frame.Rel⟩
instance {F : Frame} : Nonempty F.World := F.world_nonempty

abbrev Frame.Rel' {F : Frame} (x y : F.World) := F.Rel x y
infix:45 " ≺ " => Frame.Rel'

protected abbrev Frame.RelItr' {F : Frame} (n : ℕ) := F.Rel.iterate n
notation x:45 " ≺^[" n "] " y:46 => Frame.RelItr' n x y


structure FiniteFrame extends Frame where
  [world_finite : Finite toFrame.World]
instance {F : FiniteFrame} : Finite F.World := F.world_finite

def Frame.toFinite (F : Frame) [Finite F.World] : FiniteFrame where
  toFrame := F


abbrev reflexivePointFrame : FiniteFrame where
  World := Unit
  Rel := fun _ _ => True

abbrev irreflexivePointFrame : FiniteFrame where
  World := Unit
  Rel := fun _ _ => False


abbrev FrameClass := Set Frame

abbrev FiniteFrameClass := Set FiniteFrame

def FrameClass.restrictFinite (C : FrameClass) : FiniteFrameClass := { F : FiniteFrame | F.toFrame ∈ C }

def FiniteFrameClass.toFrameClass (C : FiniteFrameClass) : FrameClass := C.image (·.toFrame)

instance : Coe (FiniteFrameClass) (FrameClass) := ⟨FiniteFrameClass.toFrameClass⟩


section

abbrev AllFrameClass : FrameClass := Set.univ

abbrev AllFiniteFrameClass : FiniteFrameClass := Set.univ

end


abbrev Valuation (F : Frame) := F.World → ℕ → Prop

structure Model extends Frame where
  Val : Valuation toFrame

  Val : Valuation toFrame

informal_statement: For any world \( x \) and proposition \( \phi \), \( x \) satisfies \( \square \phi \) if and only if \( x \) satisfies \( \sim \diamond (\sim \phi) \).
informal_proof:
To understand the equivalence \( x \vdash \square \phi \leftrightarrow \sim \diamond (\sim \phi) \), we can break it down:

1. **Box Operator (\( \square \))**: Represents necessity. \( x \vdash \square \phi \) means that in all accessible worlds from \( x \), \( \phi \) is true.

2. **Diamond Operator (\( \diamond \))**: Represents possibility. \( x \vdash \diamond \phi \) means that there exists at least one accessible world where \( \phi \) is true.

3. **Negation (\( \sim \))**: Represents the opposite proposition. \( \sim \diamond (\sim \phi) \) means it is not possible for \( \sim \phi \) to be true in any accessible world.

The equivalence states that \( \square \phi \) holds at \( x \) **if and only if** \( \sim \diamond (\sim \phi) \) holds at \( x \). In other words, if \( \phi \) is necessarily true at \( x \), then it cannot be possibly false at any accessible world from \( x \), and vice versa.

This relationship reflects the fundamental duality between necessity and possibility in modal logic.

C1_dependencies.content:
/-- The universal set on a type `α` is the set containing all elements of `α`.

This is conceptually the "same as" `α` (in set theory, it is actually the same), but type theory
makes the distinction that `α` is a type while `Set.univ` is a term of type `Set α`. `Set.univ` can
itself be coerced to a type `↥Set.univ` which is in bijection with (but distinct from) `α`. -/
def univ : Set α := {_a | True}

informal_statement: For any world \( x \), \( x \) satisfies the modal formula \( \diamondsuit\varphi \) if and only if \( x \) satisfies \( \neg\Box(\neg\varphi) \).
informal_proof:
First, let us interpret the symbols involved. The symbol \( \diamondsuit \) denotes possibility in modal logic. Therefore, \( x \dashv\vdash \diamondsuit\varphi \) means that "in world \( x \), it is possible that \( \varphi \) holds." Similarly, \( \Box \) denotes necessity, so \( \Box(
eg\varphi) \) signifies "in all worlds, \( \varphi \) does not hold." Thus, \( 
eg\Box(
eg\varphi) \) translates to "it is not necessary that \( \varphi \) does not hold," which intuitively means "it is possible that \( \varphi \) holds in at least one world, including \( x \)."

To establish the equivalence, we will proceed in two directions:

1. **Forward Direction (\( \Rightarrow \))**: Assume \( x \dashv\vdash \diamondsuit\varphi \). By definition, this means \( \varphi \) is possible at \( x \). Consequently, it cannot be that \( \varphi \) is necessarily not true at \( x \), i.e., \( 
eg\Box(
eg\varphi) \) holds.

2. **Reverse Direction (\( \Leftarrow \))**: Suppose \( x \dashv\vdash 
eg\Box(
eg\varphi) \). This means \( \varphi \) is not necessarily false at \( x \). In other words, there exists at least one world (including \( x \)) where \( \varphi \) holds. Therefore, \( \diamondsuit\varphi \) is satisfied at \( x \).

Since both directions hold, we conclude that \( x \dashv\vdash \diamondsuit\varphi \) if and only if \( x \dashv\vdash 
eg\Box(
eg\varphi) \).

C1_dependencies.content:
/-- The universal set on a type `α` is the set containing all elements of `α`.

This is conceptually the "same as" `α` (in set theory, it is actually the same), but type theory
makes the distinction that `α` is a type while `Set.univ` is a term of type `Set α`. `Set.univ` can
itself be coerced to a type `↥Set.univ` which is in bijection with (but distinct from) `α`. -/
def univ : Set α := {_a | True}

informal_statement: If a logical implication φ → ψ holds in context x, and φ holds in context x, then ψ must also hold in context x.
informal_proof:
Given that φ → ψ holds and φ holds in context x, we can apply the rule of inference known as Modus Ponens. This rule states that if a premise implies a conclusion and the premise is true, then the conclusion must be true. Hence, since φ → ψ is true and φ is true, it logically follows that ψ is true in context x.

Therefore, the context x satisfies ψ.

informal_statement: For any context $x$, if $x$ entails that "φ implies ψ", and $x$ also entails that "ψ implies χ", then $x$ entails that "φ implies χ".
informal_proof:
Firstly, our formal statement is about the transitivity of logical implication within a specific context denoted by $x$. In simpler terms, it's saying that if having $x$ allows us to conclude that "φ implies ψ" ($x \models φ → ψ$), and we also know that $x$ allows us to conclude that "ψ implies χ" ($x \models ψ → χ$), then logically, $x$ should also enable us to conclude that "φ implies χ" ($x \models φ → χ$). This property mirrors the idea of transitivity in mathematics, where if $A$ implies $B$ and $B$ implies $C$, then $A$ implies $C$.

To break this down, we can think of it in steps:
1. Starting with φ, because we know $x$ leads to φ → ψ, we can derive ψ from having x and φ.
2. Then, since we've derived ψ from φ, and we also know that $x$ leads to ψ → χ, we can then derive χ from the previously derived ψ and the initial assumption of x.
3. Therefore, combining these steps, we effectively have that starting from x and φ, we can directly conclude χ, which is exactly what our lemma is stating.

This aligns with how logical implications can be chained together to form longer implications, ensuring that if each step is valid, the overall implication holds true. This concept is fundamental in logical reasoning and is neatly encapsulated in the transitivity of entailment (or implication) in this context.

informal_statement: For any state \( x \), the formula \( x \vdash \diamondsuit^{n}\phi \) is equivalent to the existence of a state \( y \) such that \( x \) is related to \( y \) in \( n \) steps (\( x \mathrel{\lt\!\ll}^{n} y \)) and \( y \) satisfies \( \phi \).
informal_proof:
We will prove the equivalence by induction on \( n \).

**Base Case (\( n = 0 \))**:
- **Forward Direction**: If \( x \vdash \diamondsuit^{0}\phi \), then \( x \vdash \phi \). Trivially, there exists a state \( y = x \) such that \( x \mathrel{\lt\!\ll}^{0} y \) (since zero steps mean \( x = y \)) and \( y \vdash \phi \). Thus, \( x \vdash \diamondsuit^{0}\phi \) implies the existence of such a \( y \).
- **Reverse Direction**: If there exists a state \( y \) such that \( x \mathrel{\lt\!\ll}^{0} y \) and \( y \vdash \phi \), then \( x \vdash \phi \) directly since \( y = x \).

**Inductive Step**:
Assume the statement holds for some \( n \). We will show it holds for \( n + 1 \).

**Forward Direction**:
Assume \( x \vdash \diamondsuit^{n+1}\phi \). By the definition of \( \diamondsuit^{n+1} \), there exists a state \( y \) such that \( x \mathrel{\lt\!\ll} y \) and \( y \vdash \diamondsuit^{n}\phi \). By the inductive hypothesis, since \( y \vdash \diamondsuit^{n}\phi \), there exists a state \( z \) such that \( y \mathrel{\lt\!\ll}^{n} z \) and \( z \vdash \phi \). Thus, \( x \mathrel{\lt\!\ll}^{n+1} z \) (as \( x \mathrel{\lt\!\ll} y \) and \( y \mathrel{\lt\!\ll}^{n} z \)), and \( z \vdash \phi \). Therefore, \( x \vdash \diamondsuit^{n+1}\phi \).

**Reverse Direction**:
Assume there exists a state \( z \) such that \( x \mathrel{\lt\!\ll}^{n+1} z \) and \( z \vdash \phi \). This can be decomposed into \( x \mathrel{\lt\!\ll} y \) and \( y \mathrel{\lt\!\ll}^{n} z \) for some state \( y \). By the inductive hypothesis, \( y \vdash \diamondsuit^{n}\phi \). Therefore, \( x \mathrel{\lt\!\ll} y \) and \( y \vdash \diamondsuit^{n}\phi \) implies \( x \vdash \diamondsuit^{n+1}\phi \).

By induction, the equivalence holds for all \( n \).

informal_statement:
In the context of modal logic, the statement establishes an equivalence between two conditions involving the relation \( x \perp [[n]]\varphi \) and the universal satisfaction of \( \varphi \) across all \( y \) reachable from \( x \) within \( n \) steps under the relation \( \llbracket \Box \rrbracket^{n} \).

<PROOF>

We proceed by induction on \( n \).

**Base Case ( \( n = 0 \) ):**

By definition, \( x \perp [[0]]\varphi \) holds if and only if \( x \) satisfies \( \varphi \). Since no steps are taken in the relation, this directly matches the universal statement that \( x \) satisfies \( \varphi \) for all \( y \) trivially. Thus, the equivalence holds for \( n = 0 \).

**Inductive Step:**

Assume the statement holds for some arbitrary \( n \). That is, assume:
\[
x \perp [[n]]\varphi \ \text{if and only if} \ \forall \{ y \},\ x \llbracket \Box \rrbracket^{n} y \rightarrow y \models \varphi
\]
We need to show that:
\[
x \perp [[n+1]]\varphi \ \text{if and only if} \ \forall \{ y \},\ x \llbracket \Box \rrbracket^{n+1} y \rightarrow y \models \varphi
\]
By the definition of the next-step necessity \( \Box \), \( x \llbracket \Box \rrbracket^{n+1} y \) means there exists a \( z \) such that \( x \llbracket \Box \rrbracket^{n} z \) and \( z \llbracket \Box \rrbracket y \). 

Take any \( y \) such that \( x \llbracket \Box \rrbracket^{n+1} y \). Let \( z \) witness the fact, so \( x \llbracket \Box \rrbracket^{n} z \) and \( z \llbracket \Box \rrbracket y \). By the inductive hypothesis, \( z \llbracket \Box \rrbracket y \) implies \( y \models \varphi \). Therefore, \( x \perp [[n+1]]\varphi \) implies \( y \models \varphi \).

Conversely, assume for contradiction that \( x \llbracket \Box \rrbracket^{n+1} y \) but \( y \not\models \varphi \). This leads to a contradiction with the inductive hypothesis, establishing the equivalence for \( n+1 \).

Thus, by induction, the equivalence holds for all \( n \).

</PROOF>

C1_dependencies.content:
/--
The unit type, the canonical type with one element, named `unit` or `()`.
In other words, it describes only a single value, which consists of said constructor applied
to no arguments whatsoever.
The `Unit` type is similar to `void` in languages derived from C.

`Unit` is actually defined as `PUnit.{1}` where `PUnit` is the universe
polymorphic version. The `Unit` should be preferred over `PUnit` where possible to avoid
unnecessary universe parameters.

In functional programming, `Unit` is the return type of things that "return
nothing", since a type with one element conveys no additional information.
When programming with monads, the type `m Unit` represents an action that has
some side effects but does not return a value, while `m α` would be an action
that has side effects and returns a value of type `α`.
-/
abbrev Unit : Type := PUnit

/--
The unit type, the canonical type with one element, named `unit` or `()`.
In other words, it describes only a single value, which consists of said constructor applied
to no arguments whatsoever.
The `Unit` type is similar to `void` in languages derived from C.

`Unit` is actually defined as `PUnit.{1}` where `PUnit` is the universe
polymorphic version. The `Unit` should be preferred over `PUnit` where possible to avoid
unnecessary universe parameters.

In functional programming, `Unit` is the return type of things that "return
nothing", since a type with one element conveys no additional information.
When programming with monads, the type `m Unit` represents an action that has
some side effects but does not return a value, while `m α` would be an action
that has side effects and returns a value of type `α`.
-/
abbrev Unit : Type := PUnit

informal_statement: The interpretation \( x \) satisfies the disjunction of \( \varphi \) and \( \psi \) if and only if \( x \) satisfies \( \varphi \) or \( x \) satisfies \( \psi \).
informal_proof:
To establish the equivalence \( x \vDash \varphi \lor \psi \leftrightarrow x \vDash \varphi \lor x \vDash \psi \), we proceed as follows:

First, assume that \( x \vDash \varphi \lor \psi \). By the definition of satisfaction for disjunction, this means that at least one of \( \varphi \) or \( \psi \) is true under the interpretation \( x \). Therefore, \( x \) either satisfies \( \varphi \) or satisfies \( \psi \) (or both). This directly corresponds to \( x \vDash \varphi \) or \( x \vDash \psi \).

Conversely, suppose that \( x \vDash \varphi \) or \( x \vDash \psi \). If \( x \vDash \varphi \), then by definition \( x \vDash \varphi \lor \psi \) because the disjunction is true if \( \varphi \) is true. Similarly, if \( x \vDash \psi \), then \( x \vDash \varphi \lor \psi \) because the disjunction is true if \( \psi \) is true. Thus, in either case, \( x \vDash \varphi \lor \psi \) holds.

Since both directions have been established, the equivalence is proven.

informal_statement: For any assignment \( x \), the statement \( \varphi \) implies \( \psi \) (written as \( \varphi \rightarrow \psi \)) is equivalent to the claim that if \( x \) satisfies \( \varphi \), then \( x \) also satisfies \( \psi \). This equivalence lies at the core of understanding logical implication in formal systems.
informal_proof:
To establish the equivalence between \( x \vdash \varphi \rightarrow \psi \) and \( (x \vdash \varphi) \rightarrow (x \vdash \psi) \), we proceed as follows:

1. **Definitions**: First, recall that in this logical framework, \( x \vdash \varphi \) signifies that the assignment \( x \) satisfies or models the formula \( \varphi \). Similarly, \( x \vdash \psi \) means \( x \) satisfies \( \psi \).

2. **Material Implication**: The material implication \( \varphi \rightarrow \psi \) holds under all assignments unless \( \varphi \) is true and \( \psi \) is false in a given model. In our context, this translates to \( x \vdash \varphi \rightarrow \psi \) being true unless \( x \) satisfies \( \varphi \) but does not satisfy \( \psi \).

3. **Forward Direction**: Assume \( x \vdash \varphi \rightarrow \psi \). This means there is no scenario under \( x \) where \( \varphi \) is true without \( \psi \) also being true. Therefore, if \( x \) satisfies \( \varphi \), it must also satisfy \( \psi \).

4. **Reverse Direction**: Conversely, suppose that whenever \( x \) satisfies \( \varphi \), it also satisfies \( \psi \). Under this condition, there is no assignment where \( \varphi \) is true and \( \psi \) is false, which precisely aligns with the definition of material implication. Hence, \( x \vdash \varphi \rightarrow \psi \) holds.

5. **Equivalence**: Thus, the satisfaction of \( \varphi \rightarrow \psi \) under assignment \( x \) is entirely dependent on \( x \) satisfying \( \psi \) whenever it satisfies \( \varphi \). Therefore, we have demonstrated that \( x \vdash \varphi \rightarrow \psi \) if and only if \( (x \vdash \varphi) \rightarrow (x \vdash \psi) \), completing the equivalence.

informal_statement: For any context \( x \), \( x \) satisfies the negation of \( \phi \) if and only if \( x \) does not satisfy \( \phi \).
informal_proof:
First, we interpret the formal statement `x ⊧ ∼φ ↔ ¬(x ⊧ φ)` in natural language: "For any context `x`, `x` satisfies the negation of φ if and only if `x` does not satisfy φ." This principle is known as double negation.

To prove this, we proceed by induction on φ, using the definition of satisfaction and logical negation.

Assume that `x ⊧ not φ` holds; this means `x` satisfies the formula `not φ`. By the definition of satisfaction, this is equivalent to `x` not satisfying φ, which is exactly `¬(x ⊧ φ)`.

Conversely, if `¬(x ⊧ φ)` holds, it means `x` does not satisfy φ. Therefore, `x` satisfies `not φ`.

Thus, in both directions, the satisfaction of `not φ` is equivalent to the negation of the satisfaction of φ, establishing the desired equivalence.
