informal_proof:
First, we understand that in Kripke semantics, the formula \( x \models \Diamond \phi \) (read as "It is possible that \( \phi \) at state \( x \)") means there is at least one state \( y \) accessible from \( x \) (i.e., \( x \preceq y \)) where \( y \) satisfies \( \phi \). The statement formalizes this intuition by asserting that \( x \) satisfies \( \Diamond \phi \) exactly when such a state \( y \) exists.

To see why this is true, consider the definition of \( x \models \Diamond \phi \). By definition in Kripke semantics, \( x \models \Diamond \phi \) holds if there exists a state \( y \) such that \( x \preceq y \) and \( y \) satisfies \( \phi \). This directly translates the possibility operator \( \Diamond \) into an existence claim about accessible states. Hence, the equivalence provided by the lemma is a straightforward unpacking of the definition of \( \Diamond \) in terms of accessibility and satisfaction.

The proof is thus somewhat tautological because it relies directly on the definition of satisfiability for the possibility operator. By applying the definition of \( x \models \Diamond \phi \), we directly obtain the equivalence stated in the lemma.

In summary, the lemma captures the essence of how the possibility operator \( \Diamond \) works in Kripke models by linking it to the existence of an accessible state where the formula holds. This alignment clarifies how \( \Diamond \) can be understood in terms of accessibility relations and conventional satisfaction in model checking.

informal_statement: For any world \( x \), \( x \) satisfies \( \Box\varphi \) if and only if for every world \( y \) that is accessible from \( x \), \( y \) satisfies \( \varphi \).
informal_proof:
First, we interpret the semantics of the box operator \( \Box \). By definition, in Kripke semantics, \( x \models \Box\varphi \) means that in all worlds \( y \) accessible from \( x \), \( y \) satisfies \( \varphi \). 

Breaking this down:
1. \( x \models \Box\varphi \) enforces that \( \varphi \) holds in every world \( y \) such that \( x \) can access \( y \).
2. This is precisely the statement \( \forall y (x \mathrel{\ll} y \rightarrow y \models \varphi) \), which reads as "for all \( y \), if \( y \) is accessible from \( x \), then \( y \) satisfies \( \varphi \)."

Thus, the two statements are equivalent by the very definition of \( \Box \) in Kripke semantics.

informal_statement: A Kripke model satisfies a formula $\phi$ at a world $x$ if the formula is true at that world, following the rules defined for satisfiability, necessity, and implications within the model.
informal_proof:
First, we consider atomic formulae, which are the building blocks of more complex expressions. A world $x$ in the Kripke model satisfies an atomic formula $a$ if and only if the atomic fact $a$ holds true at that world. This is formally expressed as $M, x \models \mathsf{atom}(a)$ if and only if $a$ is true at $x$, denoted by $x \in a$.

Next, for the constant false symbol $\bot$, the satisfiability condition is inherently false in all worlds. Therefore, there is no world where $M, x \models \bot$ holds.

When dealing with an implication $\phi \rightarrow \psi$, the satisfiability at a world $x$ is contingent upon $\phi$ implying $\psi$ within that same world. This means that if $M, x \models \phi$ is true, then $M, x \models \psi$ must also be true for the implication to hold.

Finally, for a formula prefixed with the necessity operator $\Box$, $\Box\phi$ is satisfied at world $x$ if and only if $\phi$ is satisfied at all worlds $y$ that are accessible from $x$ according to the accessibility relation $\preceq$. This necessity condition requires that for every $y$ such that $x \preceq y$, $M, y \models \phi$ holds true.

In summary, the satisfiability relation is defined recursively based on the syntax of the formula and the semantic relationships defined within the Kripke model. This allows for a systematic evaluation of the truth of logical formulae across different worlds in the model.

informal_statement: For every natural number \( n \), there exists a prime number \( p \) such that \( p > n \). This statement demonstrates that there are infinitely many prime numbers.
informal_proof:
First, let us consider an arbitrary natural number \( n \). Our goal is to find a prime number greater than \( n \). To achieve this, we will analyze the factorial of \( n + 1 \), denoted as \( (n + 1)! \).

Since \( (n + 1)! \) is the product of all positive integers up to \( n + 1 \), it is clear that \( (n + 1)! \geq 2 \) for all \( n \geq 1 \). This is because \( (n + 1)! = 1 \times 2 \times \ldots \times (n + 1) \), and \( 2 \) is the smallest factorial (i.e., \( 2! \)).

Next, we observe that every integer greater than 1 has at least one prime factor. Therefore, \( (n + 1)! \) must have a prime factor, say \( p \), such that \( p \leq n + 1 \). However, since \( p \) divides \( (n + 1)! \), it also divides \( (n + 1)! + 1 \) (because \( p \) divides both \( (n + 1)! \) and \( (n + 1)! + 1 \)).

Now, if we assume for contradiction that \( p \leq n \), then \( p \) would also divide the difference between \( (n + 1)! + 1 \) and \( (n + 1)! \), which is \( 1 \). This implies that \( p \) must be a divisor of \( 1 \). However, since \( p \) is a prime number, it cannot divide \( 1 \), leading to a contradiction. Therefore, our assumption that \( p \leq n \) must be false, and it follows that \( p > n \).

Having established that there exists a prime number \( p \) greater than any arbitrary natural number \( n \), we conclude that for every natural number \( n \), there exists a larger prime number \( p \). This demonstrates that the set of prime numbers is infinite.
